concepts.title: Cardiac anatomy and the path of blood
key_points: Four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle
The right side receives oxygen-poor blood from the body and sends it to the lungs
The left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and sends it to the body
Valves keep blood moving one way only
The left ventricle is the thickest chamber because it pushes blood to the whole body
Understanding the path is what makes left-sided and right-sided failure make sense
misconceptions: Believing the right side pumps to the body
Thinking oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in a normal heart
Learning the chambers without learning the direction of flow
exam_favorites: Why the left ventricle is thickest

read.plain:
The heart is two pumps in one housing, working side by side, and almost everything in cardiology makes more sense once the path is clear.

Blood coming back from the body is oxygen-poor. It arrives in the right atrium, drops into the right ventricle, and the right ventricle sends it to the lungs. In the lungs it picks up oxygen and gives up carbon dioxide.

It comes back into the left atrium, drops into the left ventricle, and the left ventricle sends it out to the entire body. Then it starts again.

Valves sit between the chambers and at the exits, and their only job is to stop blood going backwards. When they work, the circuit is one-way.

One piece of anatomy is worth noticing: the left ventricle is considerably thicker than the right. The right only has to push blood to the lungs, which are next door. The left has to push it to your toes and your brain.

Hold that circuit in mind and heart failure stops being a list to memorise. If the left side fails, blood backs up behind it into the lungs. If the right side fails, blood backs up behind it into the body. The symptoms follow from the plumbing.
read.standard: The heart comprises four chambers functioning as two pumps in series. Deoxygenated systemic venous blood enters the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle, and is ejected to the pulmonary circulation for gas exchange. Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle, and is ejected into the systemic circulation. Atrioventricular and semilunar valves maintain unidirectional flow. The left ventricular myocardium is substantially thicker than the right, reflecting the higher pressure required to perfuse the systemic rather than the pulmonary circulation. Comprehension of this circuit is prerequisite to understanding failure states, as left ventricular failure produces pulmonary congestion and right ventricular failure produces systemic venous congestion.

eli_new.analogy: Two pumps in one box. The right one delivers next door; the left one delivers to the whole country.
eli_new.body: Memorising four chamber names gets you nothing. Following one drop of blood all the way round the circuit once gets you the whole of heart failure for free.

teach.prompt: Trace a drop of blood through the heart and explain why the left ventricle is thickest.

must_hit.point: Right atrium to right ventricle to the lungs
Left atrium to left ventricle to the body
Valves keep flow one way

teach.model_answer: Oxygen-poor blood comes back from the body into the right atrium, drops into the right ventricle, and is pushed to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen. It returns to the left atrium, drops into the left ventricle, and is pushed out to the whole body. Valves between the chambers and at the exits stop it going backwards, so the circuit is one-way. The left ventricle is much thicker because the right only has to push blood next door to the lungs while the left has to reach your toes and your brain. That circuit is why left-sided failure backs up into the lungs and right-sided failure backs up into the body.

story.title: Follow the drop
story.dispatch: Training day — cardiology block, station three.
story.body:
The class had been naming chambers for twenty minutes and nobody could explain why a patient with heart failure had swollen ankles.

The instructor drew one circle on the whiteboard and traced a single drop round it with a finger, out loud, twice.

Somebody at the back said: so if the right side fails, it backs up into the body — that is the ankles. That was the whole lesson.

concepts.title: The electrical conduction system
key_points: The heart generates its own electrical impulses and does not need a nerve from the brain to beat
The normal impulse starts in the sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker
It travels to the atrioventricular node, which briefly delays it so the atria can empty into the ventricles
From there it spreads down specialised fibres through the ventricles, which contract
Lower parts of the system can take over at slower rates if the site above them fails
Electrical activity and mechanical pumping are different things: a rhythm on a monitor does not prove a pulse
misconceptions: Assuming a rhythm on the monitor means the heart is pumping
Believing the heart needs a signal from the brain to beat
Treating the delay at the AV node as a fault
exam_favorites: The AV node delay and why it exists
Electrical activity is not a pulse

read.plain:
The heart makes its own electricity. Cut every nerve to it and it will keep beating, which is why a transplanted heart works at all.

The normal impulse starts in the sinoatrial node, up in the right atrium. It is the fastest-firing site, so it sets the pace, and that is why it is called the natural pacemaker. The impulse spreads across both atria and they contract.

Then it reaches the atrioventricular node, which does something that looks like a flaw and is not: it holds the impulse for a moment. That pause is deliberate. It gives the atria time to finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles squeeze. Without the delay, all four chambers would contract at once and the pump would be far less efficient.

After the delay, the impulse runs down specialised conducting fibres into the ventricles, which contract and eject blood.

If the sinoatrial node fails, sites further down can take over, each at a slower intrinsic rate than the one above it. The heart has backups, and they are progressively slower.

One thing to hold firmly: electricity and pumping are separate. A monitor showing an organised rhythm tells you the electrical system is doing something. It does not tell you the muscle is responding. That is why you feel for a pulse, and why a patient can have a perfectly reasonable-looking rhythm on screen and no output at all.
read.standard: The myocardium possesses intrinsic automaticity and generates its own depolarising impulses independent of central nervous system input. The sinoatrial node, possessing the highest intrinsic rate, normally initiates depolarisation and functions as the dominant pacemaker. The impulse propagates across the atria producing atrial contraction, then reaches the atrioventricular node where conduction is briefly delayed, permitting completion of ventricular filling prior to ventricular systole. Conduction then proceeds through specialised ventricular conducting tissue, producing ventricular contraction. Subsidiary pacemaker sites distal to the sinoatrial node possess progressively slower intrinsic rates and assume pacemaker function on failure of more proximal sites. Electrical activity and mechanical contraction are distinct: an organised rhythm on monitoring does not establish the presence of cardiac output, which is why pulse assessment remains necessary.

eli_new.analogy: The wiring and the plumbing are separate systems. The monitor watches the wiring. Your fingers watch the plumbing.
eli_new.body: The single most important idea here is the last one. Every new provider at some point looks at an organised-looking rhythm on a screen and assumes the patient has a pulse. The screen is showing electricity. Only your fingers can tell you whether the muscle did anything about it.

teach.prompt: Describe the normal conduction pathway and explain why a rhythm on the monitor does not prove there is a pulse.

must_hit.point: SA node is the natural pacemaker
AV node delays the impulse to allow ventricular filling
Then through the ventricles, which contract
Electrical activity is not the same as mechanical pumping

teach.model_answer: The impulse starts in the sinoatrial node in the right atrium, which fires fastest and so sets the pace — the natural pacemaker. It spreads across the atria, which contract, then reaches the atrioventricular node, which deliberately holds it for a moment so the atria can finish emptying into the ventricles before they squeeze. After that delay it runs down specialised fibres through the ventricles, which contract and eject blood. If the SA node fails, sites below it take over at progressively slower rates. And electricity is not pumping: an organised rhythm on a monitor tells you the wiring is firing, not that the muscle responded, which is why you still put your fingers on a pulse.

story.title: The screen looked fine
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — collapse, CPR in progress by bystanders.
story.body:
The monitor went on and showed something organised and regular, and the room relaxed for about two seconds.

The medic did not look at the screen. She had two fingers on his neck and said, keep going.

There was no pulse. The electricity was running and the muscle was not answering, and the only thing that told anyone was a hand on a neck.

concepts.title: Cardiac output, stroke volume, preload and afterload
key_points: Cardiac output is how much blood the heart moves in a minute
Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
Stroke volume is how much blood leaves the ventricle with each beat
Preload is how full the ventricle is before it contracts
Afterload is the resistance the ventricle has to push against
A heart can compensate for falling stroke volume by increasing rate, which is why a fast pulse is an early shock sign
Compensation has limits: a rate that goes too high leaves too little filling time and output falls
misconceptions: Treating a normal heart rate as proof of adequate cardiac output
Assuming a faster rate always means more output
Confusing preload with afterload
exam_favorites: Why tachycardia is an early shock sign

read.plain:
Cardiac output is the amount of blood the heart moves in a minute, and it is the number the whole body actually cares about. It is made of two things multiplied together: how often the heart beats, and how much it ejects each time.

Stroke volume is that second part — the volume leaving the ventricle per beat. Two things shape it. Preload is how full the ventricle is when it starts to squeeze: more filling generally means more ejected, within limits. Afterload is what it has to push against: higher resistance means less gets out for the same effort.

The equation explains a great deal of what you see. A patient losing blood has less coming back to the heart, so preload falls, so stroke volume falls. Output would fall too — except the body speeds the heart up to compensate. That is exactly why tachycardia is one of the earliest signs of shock, and why it appears long before blood pressure moves.

But compensation has a ceiling. Filling happens between beats, and if the rate climbs high enough there is not enough time between beats to fill. Past that point, going faster produces less output rather than more.

And this is why a normal heart rate is not proof of adequate output. Rate is one of two terms in the equation. A normal rate with a tiny stroke volume is still a patient in trouble.
read.standard: Cardiac output is the volume of blood ejected by the heart per minute and is the product of heart rate and stroke volume. Stroke volume is determined principally by preload, the ventricular end-diastolic volume, and afterload, the resistance against which the ventricle ejects. Reduced preload, as occurs in hypovolaemia, reduces stroke volume; compensatory tachycardia maintains cardiac output and accounts for tachycardia being an early manifestation of shock, preceding measurable hypotension. Compensation is limited, as ventricular filling occurs during diastole and excessive heart rate reduces diastolic filling time sufficiently to decrease stroke volume and therefore output. A heart rate within normal limits does not establish adequate cardiac output, as rate constitutes only one determinant.

eli_new.analogy: Output is how many buckets per minute. Rate is how often you swing; stroke volume is how full the bucket is.
eli_new.body: People fixate on heart rate because it is the number that is easy to get. It is only half of the equation, and a body that is quietly compensating will hold the visible half steady while the invisible half collapses.

teach.prompt: Explain cardiac output and why a fast pulse is an early sign of shock.

must_hit.point: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume
Preload is filling; afterload is resistance
Falling stroke volume is compensated by a faster rate
Too fast leaves too little filling time

teach.model_answer: Cardiac output is how much blood the heart moves per minute, and it equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Stroke volume is what leaves the ventricle per beat, shaped by preload — how full it is before it squeezes — and afterload, the resistance it pushes against. When a patient loses blood, preload falls and stroke volume falls with it, so the body speeds the heart up to hold output steady. That is why tachycardia is one of the earliest shock signs and shows long before blood pressure moves. But filling happens between beats, so past a certain rate there is not enough time to fill and output starts falling instead. And a normal rate proves nothing on its own, because it is only one of the two terms.

story.title: Half the equation
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — 22-year-old female, fainted at work.
story.body:
Her heart rate was 118 and the student wrote it down as anxiety, which is a very popular explanation for a fast pulse in a young woman.

The paramedic asked what the other half of the equation was doing. Skin cool. Pulse thin. Pressure normal, for now.

The rate was 118 because something had taken the volume away and her body was covering for it.

concepts.title: Coronary circulation
key_points: The heart muscle does not take oxygen from the blood inside its chambers; it has its own vessels
The coronary arteries branch off the aorta immediately as it leaves the left ventricle
They fill mainly between beats rather than during the squeeze
A blocked coronary artery starves the muscle downstream of it, which is what a heart attack is
Which artery is blocked determines which part of the muscle is affected
Anything that shortens the time between beats reduces coronary filling
misconceptions: Thinking the heart is nourished by the blood passing through its chambers
Assuming coronary arteries fill during contraction
Treating chest pain as unrelated to coronary flow

read.plain:
A detail that surprises people: the heart muscle gets no oxygen at all from the blood sitting inside its chambers. It has its own supply, like any other organ.

The coronary arteries are the very first branches off the aorta, coming off within a centimetre or two of where blood leaves the left ventricle. The heart takes its cut before anybody else does, which tells you something about priority.

They fill mostly between beats. During contraction the muscle squeezes down on the vessels running through it, so flow is limited; when the muscle relaxes, the vessels open and fill. That has a practical consequence: a very fast heart rate shortens the gaps, and the gaps are when the heart feeds itself.

When one of these arteries narrows or blocks, the muscle downstream of the blockage stops getting oxygen. That is what is happening in a heart attack — not the whole heart failing, but the territory supplied by one vessel starving.

Which vessel is blocked decides which part of the muscle is affected, and that is why not every heart attack looks or behaves the same.
read.standard: Myocardial perfusion is supplied by the coronary arteries rather than by blood within the cardiac chambers. The coronary arteries arise from the aorta immediately distal to the aortic valve, receiving perfusion before the remainder of the systemic circulation. Coronary filling occurs predominantly during diastole, as systolic myocardial contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels and limits flow; tachycardia therefore reduces coronary perfusion time by shortening diastole. Occlusion of a coronary artery produces ischaemia and subsequently infarction of the myocardium supplied distal to the occlusion, constituting myocardial infarction. The distribution of injury, and consequently the clinical and electrocardiographic presentation, is determined by the vessel involved.

eli_new.analogy: The heart pays itself first, and it collects between beats, not during them.
eli_new.body: The chambers are full of oxygenated blood, so the assumption that the muscle helps itself to it is natural. It does not. The muscle is fed by pipes on the outside, and those pipes fill in the pauses.

teach.prompt: Explain how the heart muscle gets its own blood supply and why a very fast heart rate is a problem for it.

must_hit.point: Coronary arteries, not blood in the chambers
They branch off the aorta right after it leaves the left ventricle
They fill mainly between beats
A blockage starves the muscle downstream — a heart attack

teach.model_answer: The heart muscle takes nothing from the blood inside its chambers — it has its own supply through the coronary arteries, which are the very first branches off the aorta just after blood leaves the left ventricle, so the heart pays itself first. They fill mainly between beats, because during contraction the muscle squeezes the vessels running through it. That means a very fast heart rate shortens the gaps, and the gaps are exactly when the heart feeds itself. If one of those arteries narrows or blocks, the muscle downstream starves, which is what a heart attack is — and which vessel is involved decides which part of the muscle is affected.

story.title: Between the beats
story.dispatch: Training day — cardiology block, station four.
story.body:
Somebody asked why a very fast heart rate was dangerous in a patient with chest pain, given that more beats should mean more blood.

The instructor said: more beats, yes. Less time between them, though, and that is when the heart drinks.

The room went quiet for a second and then several people wrote it down.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndrome: angina and myocardial infarction
key_points: Both are caused by a coronary artery not delivering enough blood to the muscle it supplies
Angina is demand outrunning supply, usually brought on by exertion and relieved by rest
A myocardial infarction is a blockage severe enough that muscle begins to die
Pain that comes on at rest, lasts longer than usual, or is not relieved by rest is the worrying pattern
Associated findings include shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, and a feeling of impending doom
You cannot reliably tell angina from infarction in the field, and you should not try to
Time matters: muscle that stays without blood does not come back
misconceptions: Trying to distinguish angina from infarction on scene
Being reassured because the pain is not severe
Waiting to see whether rest relieves it before acting
exam_favorites: That you cannot tell them apart in the field

read.plain:
Both of these come from the same place: a coronary artery that is not delivering what the muscle behind it needs.

Angina is a mismatch. The artery is narrowed, and at rest the supply is just about adequate. Ask the muscle to work harder — climbing stairs, carrying something, an argument — and demand outruns supply, and the muscle complains. Stop, and the demand falls back, and the pain goes. That pattern of predictable exertion and relief by rest is what angina classically looks like.

A myocardial infarction is when the artery blocks badly enough that the muscle downstream is no longer getting what it needs even at rest. It begins to die. Pain arrives without exertion, lasts longer, and does not settle when they stop.

What you look for alongside the pain is the autonomic package: breathlessness, sweating, nausea, sometimes vomiting, and that particular anxious feeling patients describe as knowing something is badly wrong.

The important professional point is that you cannot tell these two apart in the field, and you must not try. The treatment pathway is the same for both, and being right about which one it was is the hospital's job, with tests you do not have. Treat the worst case and move.
read.standard: Acute coronary syndrome encompasses a spectrum of presentations arising from inadequate coronary perfusion of myocardium. Angina pectoris results from a supply-demand mismatch in the presence of coronary stenosis, characteristically precipitated by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest as demand falls. Myocardial infarction results from coronary occlusion of sufficient severity to produce myocardial necrosis, characteristically occurring at rest, of longer duration, and unrelieved by rest. Associated autonomic features include dyspnoea, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting and a subjective sense of impending doom. Prehospital differentiation between angina and infarction is not reliably achievable and is not attempted; management is directed at the more serious possibility, and delay to definitive care directly increases myocardial loss.

eli_new.analogy: Angina is the muscle complaining. Infarction is the muscle dying. From the outside they can look the same.
eli_new.body: New providers want to decide which one it is, because deciding feels like competence. The competent move is recognising that you cannot decide, treating for the worse of the two, and getting the patient to somewhere that can.

teach.prompt: Explain the difference between angina and a myocardial infarction, and why you do not try to tell them apart on scene.

must_hit.point: Both come from inadequate coronary blood supply
Angina is demand outrunning supply, relieved by rest
Infarction means muscle is dying, and rest does not fix it
You cannot reliably distinguish them in the field
Time matters

teach.model_answer: Both come from a coronary artery failing to deliver what the muscle behind it needs. In angina the artery is narrowed and supply is adequate at rest, so pain appears when demand rises with exertion and goes when they stop. In an infarction the artery is blocked badly enough that the muscle is starved even at rest, and it begins to die — so the pain comes on without exertion, lasts longer and is not relieved by rest. Alongside the pain look for breathlessness, sweating, nausea and that sense of impending doom. And you do not try to tell them apart on scene: the field treatment is the same for both and distinguishing them needs tests you do not have. Treat the worse case and move, because muscle without blood does not come back.

story.title: It went away last time
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — 64-year-old male, chest pain, at home.
story.body:
He had angina and he knew the drill: sit down, it passes.

He had been sitting down for forty minutes and it had not passed, and that was the sentence that mattered in the whole history.

He kept apologising for calling. The thing that had changed was not how bad it was. It was that rest had stopped working.

concepts.title: Atypical presentations
key_points: Many patients having a heart attack do not have classic chest pain
Women, people with diabetes and older adults are the groups most often cited for atypical presentation
Atypical presentations include shortness of breath alone, weakness, nausea or vomiting, back or jaw discomfort, and simply feeling unwell
Diabetic neuropathy can blunt the pain that would otherwise be the warning
Silent infarction happens and is more common in these groups
If the patient is in a high-risk group and something is wrong that you cannot explain, consider a cardiac cause
misconceptions: Ruling out a cardiac cause because there is no chest pain
Attributing weakness and nausea in an older patient to age or a virus
Expecting every heart attack to look like the one in the textbook

read.plain:
The classic picture — crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm — is real, and it is also not how a very large share of heart attacks arrive.

Three groups come up repeatedly. Women, people with diabetes, and older adults. Their heart attacks are more likely to present without the pain you are expecting.

What you get instead is shortness of breath with no pain at all. Or profound weakness and fatigue. Or nausea and vomiting that looks gastrointestinal. Or discomfort in the back, the jaw, the shoulder or the upper abdomen. Or, most difficult of all, a patient who simply feels unwell and cannot tell you why.

There is a mechanism behind part of this. Long-standing diabetes damages nerves, and nerves are how pain is reported. A patient whose nerves are not delivering the message can have significant muscle damage without the warning that should accompany it. Entirely silent heart attacks happen, and they happen most in exactly these groups.

So the working rule is a low threshold. A 78-year-old with diabetes who is weak, clammy and vaguely nauseated and cannot explain it has earned a cardiac workup, whatever they are or are not complaining of.
read.standard: A substantial proportion of myocardial infarctions present without classical chest pain. Atypical presentation is disproportionately represented among women, patients with diabetes mellitus and older adults. Presentations include isolated dyspnoea, profound weakness or fatigue, nausea and vomiting suggesting gastrointestinal aetiology, and discomfort referred to the back, jaw, shoulder or epigastrium; non-specific malaise may be the sole complaint. Diabetic autonomic and peripheral neuropathy attenuates nociceptive transmission, and silent infarction occurs with increased frequency in this population. A low threshold for considering acute coronary syndrome is therefore appropriate in high-risk groups presenting with unexplained symptoms irrespective of the presence of chest pain.

eli_new.analogy: The textbook heart attack is one of the ways it arrives, not the only one.
eli_new.body: The reason atypical presentations get missed is not ignorance, it is pattern matching. You are looking for the picture you were taught, and this patient does not match it, so the search stops. The fix is to make the risk group itself a trigger.

teach.model_answer: Women, people with diabetes and older adults are the groups most often cited. Instead of classic chest pain you may get shortness of breath alone, profound weakness, nausea and vomiting that looks gastrointestinal, discomfort in the back, jaw, shoulder or upper abdomen, or a patient who simply feels unwell and cannot say why. There is a mechanism in diabetes: long-standing nerve damage blunts the pain that should be the warning, so significant infarction can occur silently. The working rule is a low threshold — a high-risk patient with unexplained symptoms gets considered as cardiac whether or not they mention their chest.

story.title: Just tired
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — 78-year-old female, generally unwell, called by her daughter.
story.body:
No chest pain. None at all, and she was asked three different ways.

What she had was two days of feeling exhausted, some nausea she blamed on a sandwich, and skin that was faintly damp when you took her hand.

Diabetic for thirty years. The hospital found a substantial infarction and she never once complained of her chest.

concepts.title: Heart failure: the cardiac presentation
key_points: Heart failure means the heart cannot move blood forward well enough to meet demand
Left-sided failure backs blood up into the lungs, producing breathlessness and crackles
Right-sided failure backs blood up into the body, producing swollen ankles and distended neck veins
The two commonly occur together, because left-sided failure eventually strains the right
Patients cannot lie flat and often report sleeping on extra pillows or in a chair
Acute worsening is a common reason for a 999 call and responds to sitting the patient up and, per protocol, CPAP
misconceptions: Treating heart failure as a lung disease
Laying a breathless heart failure patient flat
Looking only for pulmonary signs and missing the peripheral ones
exam_favorites: Left versus right and where it backs up

read.plain:
Heart failure is a pump problem with consequences that show up wherever the blood is backing up, and the circuit tells you where that will be.

When the left side fails, blood stacks up behind it, and what is behind the left side is the lungs. Pressure rises in the lung vessels, fluid is squeezed into the air spaces, and the patient becomes breathless with crackles at the bases. That is the presentation you will meet most often in an emergency.

When the right side fails, blood stacks up behind it into the body. Ankles and lower legs swell. Neck veins stand out. The abdomen may become distended.

Most patients with long-standing failure have both, because a struggling left side eventually raises the pressure the right side has to push into, and the right gives way too.

The practical sign to ask about is posture. These patients cannot lie flat, because lying flat spreads the fluid across more lung. Ask how many pillows they sleep on, and whether that has changed. Moving from two pillows to three, and then to an armchair, is a story of worsening failure told in furniture.

Acute deterioration is a common call, and the immediate things that help are sitting them up, oxygen where indicated, and CPAP within your protocol.
read.standard: Heart failure denotes inadequate forward cardiac output relative to demand. Left ventricular failure produces elevated pulmonary venous pressure with transudation of fluid into the alveolar space, presenting as dyspnoea with bibasal crackles. Right ventricular failure produces systemic venous congestion, manifesting as dependent peripheral oedema, jugular venous distension and abdominal distension. Biventricular failure is common in chronic disease, as left-sided failure elevates pulmonary vascular pressure and imposes additional load on the right ventricle. Orthopnoea results from redistribution of pulmonary fluid in recumbency, and a history of increasing pillow use or sleeping upright provides useful evidence of progression. Acute decompensation is managed by upright positioning, supplemental oxygen where indicated, and continuous positive airway pressure in accordance with protocol.

eli_new.analogy: The pump fails, and the fluid piles up on whichever side of it failed.
eli_new.body: Left and right failure are easy to mix up until you connect them to the circuit. Whatever is immediately behind the failing chamber is where the fluid goes: behind the left is the lungs, behind the right is the body.

teach.prompt: Explain the difference between left-sided and right-sided heart failure and why these patients cannot lie flat.

must_hit.point: Left failure backs up into the lungs
Right failure backs up into the body
Both often coexist
Lying flat spreads fluid across more lung

teach.model_answer: Heart failure means the pump cannot move blood forward well enough, and the symptoms appear wherever blood backs up. Behind the left side are the lungs, so left-sided failure causes breathlessness and crackles at the bases. Behind the right side is the body, so right-sided failure causes swollen ankles, distended neck veins and sometimes a distended abdomen. Most long-standing patients have both, because a failing left side raises the pressure the right has to work against. They cannot lie flat because lying flat spreads the fluid across more lung — so ask about pillows, and whether that has changed, because two pillows becoming three and then an armchair is the story of the illness. Acutely, sit them up, give oxygen where indicated, and use CPAP within protocol.

story.title: Told in furniture
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — 81-year-old male, difficulty breathing, worse for three nights.
story.body:
The useful part of the history was not about his chest at all.

He used to sleep on one pillow. Three months ago it became two. Last week it became three, and for the last three nights he had been sleeping in the armchair by the window.

His ankles were over the tops of his slippers. Nobody needed a test to know which way this had been going.

concepts.title: Cardiogenic shock
key_points: Shock caused by the heart itself failing as a pump, most often after a large myocardial infarction
The patient has enough blood; the pump cannot move it
Findings are the usual shock picture — pale, cool, clammy, altered mental status — plus signs of a failing heart
Unlike hypovolaemic shock, the neck veins are often distended rather than flat
Fluid is not the answer here and can make it worse by flooding lungs that are already congested
EMT care is oxygen, position, rapid transport and early ALS; the definitive treatment is in hospital
Mortality is high and recognition matters more than anything an EMT can do at the roadside
misconceptions: Treating cardiogenic shock with fluids as though it were blood loss
Expecting flat neck veins in every shocked patient
Laying a patient with pulmonary congestion flat
exam_favorites: Pump failure rather than volume loss
Distended rather than flat neck veins

read.plain:
Cardiogenic shock is the heart failing so badly as a pump that the rest of the body stops being perfused. The commonest cause is a large heart attack that has destroyed enough muscle that what remains cannot do the job.

The crucial difference from the shock you may be more used to is the volume. In bleeding, there is not enough blood. Here there is plenty of blood; the pump simply cannot move it. That single difference changes what helps and what harms.

The patient looks shocked in the familiar ways — pale, cool, clammy, confused or drowsy, with a fast weak pulse and eventually a falling blood pressure. What is added is evidence that the heart is the problem: often chest pain or a recent history of it, breathlessness, crackles, and neck veins that are distended rather than flat, because blood is backing up behind a failing pump.

That neck vein finding is the one worth carrying. A shocked patient with flat neck veins is usually short of volume. A shocked patient with full neck veins usually is not, and giving them fluid can flood lungs that are already wet.

An EMT's contribution here is recognition, oxygen, an upright position if the lungs are congested, minimal delay, and ALS as early as possible. This is a condition where the useful thing you do is get them somewhere that can help.
read.standard: Cardiogenic shock is hypoperfusion resulting from primary failure of myocardial pump function, most commonly following extensive myocardial infarction. Circulating volume is adequate; the deficit is in forward output. Presentation combines the general features of shock — pallor, cool diaphoretic skin, altered mental status, tachycardia with weak pulses and eventual hypotension — with evidence of cardiac aetiology including chest pain, dyspnoea, pulmonary crackles and jugular venous distension. Distended rather than flat neck veins distinguish it from hypovolaemic shock and indicate that volume administration is inappropriate and potentially harmful, as fluid loading exacerbates pulmonary congestion. Prehospital management comprises recognition, oxygen, appropriate positioning, minimised scene time and early advanced life support activation; mortality remains high and definitive management is in hospital.

eli_new.analogy: In bleeding, the tank is empty. In cardiogenic shock, the tank is full and the pump has failed.
eli_new.body: The neck veins are the quickest way to separate the two in your head. Empty tank, flat veins. Failed pump, full veins. That one observation changes whether fluid helps or harms.

teach.model_answer: It is shock caused by the heart failing as a pump, usually after a large heart attack destroyed enough muscle that what is left cannot do the job. The key difference from bleeding is that there is plenty of blood — the pump just cannot move it. The patient looks shocked in the usual ways, pale, cool, clammy, altered, with a fast weak pulse, but with cardiac evidence added: chest pain or recent chest pain, breathlessness, crackles, and neck veins that are distended rather than flat. That is the quickest discriminator — flat veins means an empty tank, full veins means a failed pump — and it matters because fluid helps the first and floods the lungs of the second. Your contribution is recognition, oxygen, upright positioning if the lungs are wet, minimal delay and early ALS.

story.title: Full veins
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — 69-year-old male, collapse, chest pain earlier today.
story.body:
He was shocked by every measure. Grey, wet, confused, thready at 130.

The student reached for the reasoning she knew: shocked patient, give fluid.

The officer pointed at his neck. The veins were standing out like cords, and his chest was full of crackles. This was a pump that had stopped working, not a tank that had emptied, and a litre of fluid would have gone straight into his lungs.

concepts.title: Hypertensive emergency
key_points: A very high blood pressure that is causing damage to organs right now
The number alone does not make it an emergency; the evidence of damage does
Warning features include severe headache, visual disturbance, chest pain, breathlessness, altered mental status, seizure and one-sided weakness
Many people live with chronically high readings and are not in an emergency

Ignoring a high number in a patient with neurological findings
Attempting to reduce blood pressure at the roadside
exam_favorites: That chronic hypertension is not an emergency

read.plain:
A hypertensive emergency is not defined by how big the number is. It is defined by a very high blood pressure that is actively damaging organs at the moment you are standing there.

That distinction matters because a great many people walk around with readings that would alarm you and are not in any immediate danger. A number on its own, in a patient who feels well and has no findings, is a number.

What turns it into an emergency is evidence. A severe headache, particularly one described as the worst ever. Disturbed vision. Chest pain. Breathlessness. Confusion or altered mental status. A seizure. Weakness or numbness down one side. These say the pressure is doing harm to a brain, a heart or a kidney, and that patient needs to move.

Your job is not to fix the pressure. There is nothing an EMT carries that safely lowers blood pressure, and lowering it too quickly is itself dangerous. Keep them calm, let them sit how they are comfortable, give oxygen if indicated, and transport.

When you hand over, give the number and the findings together. A systolic reading with no context invites the wrong conclusion in either direction.
read.standard: Hypertensive emergency denotes severe blood pressure elevation accompanied by evidence of acute end-organ damage, and is defined by the presence of that damage rather than by the absolute value. Chronic asymptomatic hypertension is common and does not constitute an emergency. Features indicating end-organ involvement include severe headache, visual disturbance, chest pain, dyspnoea, altered mental status, seizure and focal neurological deficit, reflecting cerebral, cardiac or renal injury. Prehospital management is supportive: reduction of anxiety, position of comfort, supplemental oxygen where indicated and transport. Attempts to reduce blood pressure in the prehospital environment are not undertaken, as abrupt reduction carries its own risk. Handover should communicate the measured value together with the associated clinical findings.

eli_new.analogy: The number is not the emergency. What the number is doing to the organs is the emergency.
eli_new.body: A very high reading produces an urge to do something about the reading. There is nothing to do about the reading. The useful question is whether this pressure is currently hurting a brain, a heart or a kidney, and that is answered by looking at the patient rather than the cuff.

teach.model_answer: It is a very high pressure that is actively damaging organs right now, and it is the damage rather than the number that defines it — plenty of people live with readings that would alarm you and are in no immediate danger. The evidence you look for is a severe headache, disturbed vision, chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, a seizure, or one-sided weakness, all of which say a brain, heart or kidney is being harmed. You do not try to lower the pressure: nothing an EMT carries does that safely, and dropping it too fast is dangerous in itself. Keep them calm, let them sit comfortably, oxygen if indicated, transport — and hand over the number and the findings together.

story.title: Two hundred and ten

The systolic reading was high enough that the student went quiet.

What mattered was not the number. It was that he said this was the worst headache of his life, that the light was hurting his eyes, and that his wife said he had been muddling his words for about an hour.

The same number, in a man with no symptoms, would have been a different call entirely.

concepts.title: Aortic aneurysm and dissection
key_points: The aorta is the largest artery in the body, leaving the left ventricle
An aneurysm is a weakened, bulging section of the wall; a dissection is a tear allowing blood between the layers
Classic dissection pain is sudden, severe, tearing or ripping, often described as the worst pain of the patient's life
Pain in the chest may radiate to the back and between the shoulder blades
A difference in blood pressure or pulse between the two arms is a suggestive finding
An abdominal aneurysm may present as back or abdominal pain with a pulsating mass
Do not palpate deeply or repeatedly if you suspect an abdominal aneurysm
There is nothing an EMT can do but recognise, handle gently, and move fast
misconceptions: Deeply palpating a suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm
Dismissing tearing back pain as musculoskeletal
Failing to check both arms when dissection is suspected
exam_favorites: Tearing pain radiating to the back

read.plain:
The aorta is the main pipe out of the heart, and its problems are among the most lethal things you will meet.

An aneurysm is a section of the wall that has weakened and ballooned outward. A dissection is a tear in the inner lining that lets blood force its way between the layers of the wall, splitting them apart. Both can rupture, and rupture is usually rapidly fatal.

The pain is the thing patients remember. Sudden, severe, and described as tearing or ripping rather than crushing. It often starts in the chest and goes through to the back, between the shoulder blades. Patients frequently say it is the worst pain they have ever had, and they often can tell you the exact second it started.

One physical finding is worth knowing: a significant difference in blood pressure or pulse strength between the two arms, which can happen when the dissection involves the vessels supplying one arm.

An abdominal aneurysm presents differently — abdominal or back pain, sometimes with a pulsating mass in the abdomen. If you suspect one, do not go pressing on it. Deep or repeated palpation of a weakened aortic wall is exactly what you do not want to do.

There is no field treatment. Recognise it, handle the patient gently, give oxygen if indicated, do not delay, and tell the hospital what you are worried about.
read.standard: The aorta is the principal systemic artery arising from the left ventricle. Aortic aneurysm denotes pathological dilatation of a weakened arterial wall; aortic dissection denotes an intimal tear permitting blood to enter and separate the layers of the arterial wall. Both carry risk of rupture with high associated mortality. Dissection characteristically produces abrupt, severe pain described as tearing or ripping, frequently anterior with radiation to the interscapular region, and of an intensity patients identify as unprecedented with a precisely identifiable onset. A significant differential in blood pressure or pulse quality between the upper limbs is a suggestive finding where the dissection involves the origin of a subclavian vessel. Abdominal aortic aneurysm may present with abdominal or back pain and a pulsatile mass; deep or repeated palpation is contraindicated. No prehospital intervention alters the pathology; management comprises recognition, gentle handling, oxygen where indicated, expedited transport and early notification.

eli_new.analogy: Crushing is the word for a heart attack. Tearing is the word that should make you think of the aorta.
eli_new.body: The word patients choose does real diagnostic work here. Nobody describes angina as ripping. When someone reaches for tearing, ripping or splitting, and can tell you the exact moment it began, that vocabulary should move the aorta up your list.

Both can rupture and rupture is usually fatal. The pain is sudden, severe, and described as tearing or ripping rather than crushing, often starting in the chest and going through to the back between the shoulder blades, and patients often know the exact second it started. A meaningful difference in blood pressure or pulse between the two arms is suggestive, so check both. If you suspect an abdominal aneurysm, do not palpate deeply or repeatedly — pressing on a weakened aortic wall is the last thing you want to do. There is no field treatment: recognise, handle gently, move, and tell the hospital.

He said it felt like something had torn. Not crushing, not pressure — torn, and he could name the minute.

It had started between his shoulder blades and come round to the front.

The blood pressure in his right arm and his left arm were not close to each other, and that was the finding that went in the pre-alert.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest causes and sudden cardiac death
key_points: Cardiac arrest is the heart stopping effective pumping; the patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no pulse
Sudden cardiac death most often follows a lethal rhythm disturbance, frequently triggered by a heart attack
Other causes include respiratory failure, severe blood loss, electrolyte problems, drowning, electrocution, overdose and hypothermia
In adults the commonest path is a primary cardiac event; in children it is more often respiratory
Agonal gasps are common in the first minutes and are frequently mistaken for breathing
The interventions that change outcome are early recognition, early compressions and early defibrillation
misconceptions: Mistaking agonal gasps for breathing and delaying compressions
Assuming a pediatric arrest has the same cause as an adult one
Searching for a cause before starting compressions

read.plain:
Cardiac arrest means the heart has stopped pumping effectively. The patient is unresponsive, is not breathing normally, and has no pulse, and those three findings together are the whole definition.

In adults, the commonest route is a lethal rhythm disturbance — the electrical system degenerates into something that quivers instead of pumping — and the commonest trigger for that is a heart attack. That is what sudden cardiac death usually is.

There are other causes, and it is worth holding them loosely in mind: respiratory failure that went on too long, catastrophic blood loss, electrolyte disturbances, drowning, electrocution, overdose and severe hypothermia.

The age difference matters. Adults arrest from their hearts. Children much more often arrest from their breathing — a respiratory problem that was not fixed, which eventually starves the heart. That is why airway and ventilation carry more weight in a pediatric arrest.

One recognition point causes more delay than anything else: agonal gasps. In the first minutes after an arrest, many patients make slow, irregular, gulping movements. They look like breathing to anyone who has not seen them before, and they are not. A patient who is unresponsive and making those movements is in arrest.

And resist the urge to work out why before you start. The things that change outcomes are recognising it, starting compressions, and getting a defibrillator on. The cause can be considered while the compressions are already happening.
read.standard: Cardiac arrest denotes cessation of effective cardiac output, identified by unresponsiveness, absence of normal breathing and absence of a palpable pulse. In adults, sudden cardiac death most commonly results from malignant dysrhythmia, frequently precipitated by acute myocardial infarction. Additional aetiologies include respiratory failure, exsanguination, electrolyte disturbance, submersion, electrocution, toxic ingestion and severe hypothermia. Aetiology differs by age: adult arrest is predominantly of primary cardiac origin, whereas pediatric arrest more commonly results from progressive respiratory failure, which alters the emphasis placed on airway and ventilation. Agonal respiration occurs frequently in the early minutes following arrest and is commonly misinterpreted as effective breathing, producing delay in initiating compressions. Outcome is determined principally by early recognition, early chest compressions and early defibrillation rather than by identification of the underlying cause.

eli_new.analogy: Three findings and you are done deciding: unresponsive, not breathing normally, no pulse. Start.
eli_new.body: The gap between an arrest happening and compressions starting is almost entirely made of hesitation, and most of that hesitation is somebody watching agonal gasps and wondering whether that counts as breathing. It does not.

teach.model_answer: Cardiac arrest is the heart no longer pumping effectively, and the definition is three findings together: unresponsive, not breathing normally, no pulse. In adults it usually comes from a lethal rhythm disturbance, most often triggered by a heart attack — that is what sudden cardiac death generally is. Other causes include respiratory failure, major blood loss, electrolyte problems, drowning, electrocution, overdose and hypothermia. In children the cause is far more often respiratory, a breathing problem that was not fixed, which is why airway and ventilation matter more in a paediatric arrest. Agonal gasps — slow irregular gulping in the first minutes — look like breathing to anyone who has not seen them, and mistaking them is the commonest source of delay. What changes outcome is early recognition, early compressions and early defibrillation, not working out the cause first.

story.title: Eleven seconds
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — collapse in a supermarket, staff on scene.
story.body:
The staff member said he was still breathing, and from where she was standing he was: big, slow, gulping movements every ten seconds or so.

Your partner had two fingers on his neck before the sentence finished and said, no pulse, starting.

Eleven seconds from door to first compression. Everything that mattered on that call had already happened by the time anybody wondered why he had arrested.

concepts.title: Assisting with aspirin and nitroglycerin
key_points: Both are assisted rather than administered independently, within protocol and often with medical direction
Aspirin is given for suspected acute coronary syndrome because it reduces clot formation
Aspirin is withheld where there is an allergy, or per protocol where there is active bleeding or a bleeding disorder
Aspirin is chewed rather than swallowed whole so it acts faster
Nitroglycerin dilates blood vessels and reduces the heart's workload, and is assisted with the patient's own prescribed medication
Nitroglycerin can drop blood pressure sharply, so a blood pressure is checked before and after every dose
Nitroglycerin is contraindicated where the patient has recently taken erectile dysfunction medication, because the combination can cause a catastrophic fall in pressure
Always run the six rights before assisting
misconceptions: Assisting with nitroglycerin without checking a blood pressure first
Failing to ask about erectile dysfunction medication because it feels awkward
Assisting with medication prescribed to somebody else
Giving aspirin to swallow whole
exam_favorites: Blood pressure before and after nitroglycerin

read.plain:
Two medications an EMT may assist with in a cardiac call. Neither is carried and administered on your own authority: you are helping a patient take something, within protocol and usually after speaking to medical direction.

Aspirin is given because it makes platelets less likely to clump, which matters when the problem is a clot forming in a coronary artery. The practical detail is that it is chewed rather than swallowed, because chewing gets it working sooner. You withhold it for a known allergy, and per your protocol where there is active bleeding or a bleeding disorder.

Nitroglycerin relaxes blood vessels. That reduces how hard the heart has to work and can relieve the pain of angina. You are assisting with the patient's own prescription.

And it has a consequence that dictates the whole procedure: it can drop blood pressure sharply. So you take a blood pressure before every dose and after every dose, and you follow the thresholds in your protocol about when not to give it.

There is one interaction that has to be asked about explicitly. Erectile dysfunction medications work in a related way, and taken together with nitroglycerin they can produce a catastrophic and sometimes fatal fall in blood pressure. This question is awkward and it is not optional. Ask it directly, ask it out of earshot of family, and ask it of every patient, regardless of age or who is in the room.

And run the six rights before assisting with either.
read.standard: Aspirin and nitroglycerin are administered at EMT level by assisting the patient, under protocol and commonly with online medical direction. Aspirin exerts antiplatelet effect and is indicated in suspected acute coronary syndrome; it is chewed rather than swallowed to accelerate absorption. Contraindications include known hypersensitivity and, per protocol, active haemorrhage or bleeding disorder. Nitroglycerin produces vasodilation, reducing myocardial workload and relieving anginal pain, and is assisted using the patient's own prescribed supply. Because nitroglycerin may produce marked hypotension, blood pressure is measured before and after each dose and protocol thresholds observed. Concurrent use of phosphodiesterase inhibitors prescribed for erectile dysfunction constitutes a contraindication, as the combination may precipitate profound and potentially fatal hypotension; this history must be elicited directly, privately and from every patient irrespective of age. The six rights are verified prior to assisting with either medication.

eli_new.analogy: Nitroglycerin opens the pipes. If someone has already taken something else that opens the pipes, the pressure has nowhere to go.
eli_new.body: The erectile dysfunction question is skipped constantly, because it is embarrassing to ask and people assume it does not apply to the patient in front of them. It is asked of everybody, quietly, away from the family, because the consequence of not asking can be fatal.

teach.model_answer: You are assisting with the patient's own prescribed medication, under protocol and usually after medical direction, and you run the six rights first. Aspirin is chewed rather than swallowed because chewing gets it absorbed and working sooner; you withhold it for a known allergy and, per protocol, for active bleeding or a bleeding disorder. Nitroglycerin relaxes blood vessels and reduces the heart's workload, but it can drop blood pressure sharply, so you take a blood pressure before and after every single dose and follow your protocol's thresholds. And you must ask directly about erectile dysfunction medication, because the combination can cause a catastrophic fall in pressure. Ask it of every patient, quietly and out of earshot of family, however awkward it feels.

The medic asked the daughter to fetch his medication list from upstairs, which she did, and which took about ninety seconds.

In those ninety seconds he asked the question, quietly, and the answer was yes, last night.

He was seventy-two and his daughter was in the house and it would have been very easy not to ask. The nitroglycerin did not get given.

concepts.title: The chain of survival
key_points: A sequence of actions, each of which loses value if the ones before it are missing
Recognition of arrest and activation of emergency response comes first
Early high-quality CPR is the second link and buys time for everything after it
Early defibrillation is the link that most often converts a shockable rhythm
Advanced care and post-arrest care follow
Recovery is now recognised as part of the chain rather than the end of it
Bystander action on the first two links does more for survival than anything an EMT adds later
misconceptions: Treating defibrillation as the only link that matters
Believing survival begins when the ambulance arrives
Delaying compressions to prepare equipment

read.plain:
The chain of survival is a way of saying that cardiac arrest survival is not one intervention, it is a sequence, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

It starts with somebody recognising that this is an arrest and calling for help. Nothing else can begin until that happens, and delay here is the single commonest reason people die.

Then early, high-quality CPR. Compressions do not usually restart a heart. What they do is keep some blood moving to the brain and the heart muscle itself, which keeps the heart in a state where a shock might still work. Compressions buy time for the next link.

Then early defibrillation. For a shockable rhythm, this is the intervention that actually converts it, and every minute of delay reduces the chance.

Then advanced care, and then the care that happens after the heart restarts, which is where a great deal of the eventual outcome is decided. Recovery is now included as a link in its own right, recognising that surviving to hospital discharge is not the end of the story.

The uncomfortable truth for professionals is that the first two links belong to bystanders, and they matter more than anything you will do. A patient who had compressions from a stranger within a minute has a different outcome from one who waited eight minutes for you.
read.standard: The chain of survival describes the sequence of interventions determining outcome in cardiac arrest, in which the effectiveness of later interventions depends on the timely completion of earlier ones. The links comprise recognition of arrest and activation of the emergency response system; early high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation; early defibrillation; advanced resuscitative care; post-cardiac-arrest care; and recovery. Chest compressions rarely restore spontaneous circulation independently but maintain coronary and cerebral perfusion, preserving myocardial viability and the likelihood of successful defibrillation. Survival declines with each minute of delay to defibrillation in shockable rhythms. The initial links are predominantly executed by lay responders, and bystander recognition and compression have a greater aggregate effect on survival than subsequent professional interventions.

eli_new.analogy: Compressions do not usually restart the heart. They keep it worth shocking.
eli_new.body: The instinct is to think of the defibrillator as the thing that saves people, and the compressions as what you do while waiting for it. It is closer to the opposite: compressions are what keep the patient in a condition where the shock can still work.

Compressions rarely restart a heart — what they do is keep blood moving to the brain and to the heart muscle itself, which keeps the heart in a state where a shock can still work. So compressions buy time for defibrillation rather than substituting for it. And the uncomfortable part is that the first two links belong to bystanders, and a patient who got compressions from a stranger within a minute has a very different outcome from one who waited eight minutes for an ambulance.

story.title: Before you arrived
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — cardiac arrest, bystander CPR in progress, gym.
story.body:
By the time you were through the door, a personal trainer had been doing compressions for four minutes and somebody had run for the AED on the wall.

He survived, and he walked out of hospital nine days later.

The crew got the credit. What actually decided it had already happened before the ambulance turned into the car park.

key_points: Confirm unresponsiveness, absent normal breathing and no pulse, then start compressions immediately
Hands on the lower half of the sternum, heel of one hand with the other on top

Compress at least 2 inches (5 cm) and no more than 2.4 inches (6 cm) in an adult
Allow full chest recoil between compressions; leaning on the chest reduces filling

read.plain:
Adult CPR begins the moment you have your three findings: unresponsive, not breathing normally, no pulse. Do not go looking for anything else first.

Hands go on the lower half of the sternum, heel of one hand with the other stacked on top, arms straight, shoulders over your hands so your body weight does the work rather than your arms.

The numbers matter. Compress at 100 to 120 per minute. Go at least 2 inches — 5 centimetres — deep, and not more than about 2.4 inches, or 6 centimetres. Too shallow does not move blood; too deep causes injury without benefit.

Let the chest come all the way back up between compressions. This is the detail most commonly done badly. If you lean on the chest, it cannot refill, and you are compressing an empty heart. Full recoil is as important as depth.

Ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths in an adult, whether you are alone or working with somebody.

Keep every interruption under 10 seconds. Everything — rhythm checks, moving the patient, placing an adjunct — is measured against that limit.

And swap whoever is compressing roughly every 2 minutes. Quality falls off long before the person doing it notices, and they will tell you they are fine. Swap anyway.

Once an advanced airway is in place, the ratio disappears. Compressions become continuous, and ventilation runs alongside at one breath every 6 seconds.
read.standard: Adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation is initiated immediately upon identification of unresponsiveness, absent normal breathing and absent pulse. Hand position is the lower half of the sternum, with the heel of one hand and the second hand superimposed, elbows extended and shoulders positioned above the hands. Compression rate is 100 to 120 per minute at a depth of at least 5 cm and not exceeding approximately 6 cm. Complete chest recoil between compressions is required, as residual leaning impairs ventricular filling and reduces the efficacy of subsequent compressions. The compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2 for single- and two-rescuer adult CPR. Interruptions are limited to under 10 seconds. Compressor rotation approximately every 2 minutes is recommended, as compression quality deteriorates before the provider perceives fatigue. Following advanced airway placement, compressions are delivered continuously with ventilation at one breath every 6 seconds.

eli_new.analogy: Push hard, push fast, let it all the way back up, and do not stop.
eli_new.body: Of the four things that make compressions good — depth, rate, recoil and minimal interruption — recoil is the one people get wrong without knowing it. Leaning feels like commitment. It is actually stopping the heart from refilling.

teach.model_answer: Start as soon as you have unresponsive, not breathing normally and no pulse. Heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum with the other on top, arms straight, shoulders over your hands. Compress 100 to 120 per minute, at least 2 inches or 5 centimetres deep and no more than about 2.4 inches or 6 centimetres. Ratio is 30 to 2 whether you are alone or with a partner. The two things people get wrong are recoil and interruptions: leaning on the chest stops it refilling so you are compressing an empty heart, and every pause should be under 10 seconds. Swap compressors about every 2 minutes, because quality drops well before the person notices. Once there is an advanced airway, compressions become continuous with a breath every 6 seconds.

story.title: I'm fine
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — cardiac arrest, residence, long carry down.
story.body:
He had been compressing for nearly four minutes and he said he was fine, because everybody says they are fine.

The officer watched the chest rather than the man. The compressions were still fast and they were no longer deep, and the chest was not coming all the way back up.

They swapped mid-count. The difference in the waveform on the monitor was visible within three compressions.

concepts.title: Child and infant CPR differences
key_points: A child is from about one year to puberty; an infant is under one year
Rate is the same at all ages: 100 to 120 per minute
Child depth is about 2 inches (5 cm), or at least one third of the chest depth
Infant depth is about 1.5 inches (4 cm), or at least one third of the chest depth
Child compressions use one or two hands; infant compressions use two fingers, or two thumbs with hands encircling the chest for two rescuers
Ratio is 30:2 with a single rescuer and 15:2 with two rescuers in children and infants
Pediatric arrest is more often respiratory, so ventilation matters more than in adults
Check a brachial pulse in an infant rather than a carotid
misconceptions: Using the adult 30:2 ratio with two rescuers on a child
Compressing an infant too shallowly for fear of causing harm
Neglecting ventilation in a pediatric arrest
exam_favorites: Depth as a fraction of chest depth

read.plain:
Children are not small adults in arrest either, and several numbers change.

Definitions first, because the ratios depend on them. An infant is under one year. A child runs from about one year to the onset of puberty. After that, treat them as an adult.

What does not change is rate: 100 to 120 per minute at every age.

Depth does change, and it is expressed two ways. For a child, about 2 inches or 5 centimetres, or at least one third of the depth of the chest. For an infant, about 1.5 inches or 4 centimetres, or again at least one third. The one-third rule is the more useful version, because it scales to the child in front of you.

Hand position changes. A child gets one hand, or two if you need them. An infant gets two fingers if you are alone, or the two-thumb encircling technique if there are two of you, which produces better compressions.

The ratio is the thing most often got wrong. Alone, it is 30:2, same as an adult. With two rescuers on a child or an infant, it becomes 15:2 — more breaths, more often.

That ratio change is not arbitrary. Children arrest from respiratory causes far more often than adults do, so ventilation carries more of the work. In an adult arrest, compressions dominate; in a child, breathing is nearer the heart of the problem.

One practical detail: an infant pulse is checked at the brachial artery in the upper arm, not the neck.
read.standard: Pediatric resuscitation parameters differ by age category: infant denotes under one year and child from approximately one year to the onset of puberty, beyond which adult parameters apply. Compression rate remains 100 to 120 per minute across all ages. Compression depth is approximately 5 cm in the child and approximately 4 cm in the infant, or at least one third of the anteroposterior chest diameter, the latter formulation scaling appropriately to patient size. Child compressions employ one or two hands; infant compressions employ the two-finger technique for single rescuers or the two-thumb encircling-hands technique for two rescuers, the latter producing superior compression quality. The compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2 for single-rescuer and 15:2 for two-rescuer pediatric resuscitation, reflecting the predominantly respiratory aetiology of pediatric arrest. Infant pulse assessment is performed at the brachial artery.

eli_new.analogy: Adults arrest from the heart; children arrest from the breathing. The ratio change is that fact written down.
eli_new.body: The 15:2 ratio is the single most commonly missed number in pediatric resuscitation, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising: children need more ventilation because breathing is usually what failed first.

story.title: Fifteen and two
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — 8-month-old, unresponsive, not breathing, home.
story.body:
Two of you, an infant, and the new EMT started counting to thirty out of pure muscle memory.

The officer said fifteen, without breaking rhythm, and they reset.

He had been drilled on adults for six months. Nothing about the room told him this was different except the size of the patient, and the number that changes is the one nobody practises.

concepts.title: Using an AED
key_points: Apply it as soon as it arrives; do not finish a cycle first
Turn it on and follow the prompts — the device drives the sequence
Bare the chest and dry it if wet; pads do not stick to water or sweat
Standard adult pad placement is upper right chest and lower left side
Use pediatric pads or a pediatric setting for children under 8 where available; if not available, adult pads may be used rather than withholding defibrillation
Nobody touches the patient while it analyses or shocks — say it out loud and look before you press
Resume compressions immediately after the shock without checking a pulse first
Remove a medication patch under a pad, and place pads away from an implanted device
misconceptions: Delaying pad placement to finish a cycle of compressions
Shocking without visually confirming everyone is clear
Withholding defibrillation from a child because pediatric pads are unavailable
Placing a pad directly over a medication patch or a pacemaker
exam_favorites: Resume compressions immediately after the shock

read.plain:
The defibrillator is the link that converts shockable rhythms, and everything about using one is designed around getting it on fast and not interrupting compressions more than you must.

When it arrives, apply it. Do not finish the cycle you are in. Turn it on and do what it tells you; the machine runs the sequence and it is designed to be used by people with far less training than you.

The chest has to be bare and dry. Pads will not stick through water, sweat or a hairy chest, and a pad that is not stuck is a shock that does not reach the heart.

Standard adult placement is one pad on the upper right chest below the collarbone and one on the lower left side, below and lateral to the left nipple.

For children under about 8, use pediatric pads or a pediatric setting if you have them. If you do not have them, use the adult pads. An imperfect shock is better than no shock, and withholding defibrillation from a child in a shockable rhythm because the right pads were not in the bag is the worse error.

Clearing is the part where discipline matters. Nobody touches the patient while the machine analyses and nobody touches during the shock. Say it out loud, and then actually look — at the head, at the feet, at your own knees. People have been shocked because somebody announced clear without checking.

After the shock, go straight back to compressions. Do not pause to check a pulse. The rhythm check comes at the next cycle.

Two details worth knowing: peel off a medication patch that is under where a pad needs to go, and place pads slightly away from an obvious implanted pacemaker or defibrillator.
read.standard: Automated external defibrillator application should occur immediately upon arrival of the device rather than at completion of a compression cycle. The device is activated and its prompts followed. The chest must be exposed and dried, as pad adhesion is compromised by moisture and excessive chest hair, and inadequate adhesion impairs energy delivery. Standard adult pad placement is anterolateral, with one pad inferior to the right clavicle and the second at the left mid-axillary line below the nipple. Pediatric pads or a pediatric attenuating setting should be used in children under approximately eight years where available; where unavailable, adult pads are used rather than withholding defibrillation. All personnel must be clear of the patient during analysis and shock delivery, confirmed both verbally and visually. Chest compressions are resumed immediately following shock delivery without an intervening pulse check. Transdermal medication patches beneath the pad site are removed, and pads are positioned away from implanted cardiac devices.

eli_new.analogy: The machine will tell you what to do. Your jobs are to get it on fast, keep everyone off the patient, and go straight back to compressions.
eli_new.body: The hardest habit is resuming compressions the instant the shock is delivered. Everyone wants to look for a pulse, because that is the moment they have been waiting for. Looking costs seconds, and seconds of no compressions is exactly what the whole procedure is built to avoid.

story.title: Say it and look
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — arrest in a corridor, AED from the wall in use.
story.body:
The crew member called clear and pressed the button in the same breath, which is how it is usually done and how it should never be done.

A family member had reached in from behind to touch his father's shoulder and got a jolt up the arm for it. Not a serious one. It could have been.

After that, in that service, clear meant saying it, then looking head, feet and your own knees, and then pressing.

concepts.title: High-performance CPR and pit-crew roles
key_points: High-performance CPR treats resuscitation as a choreographed team activity rather than a set of individual tasks
Every person has a defined role before the call, so nobody negotiates on scene
Compression fraction — the proportion of time compressions are actually happening — is the measure that matters most
Changeovers are planned and rehearsed so they cost seconds rather than tens of seconds
One person runs the resuscitation and does not have their hands on the patient
Quality is measured, not assumed, and feedback devices are used where available
misconceptions: Deciding roles on scene while the patient is in arrest
Treating compression pauses as unavoidable
Having the team leader also performing compressions
exam_favorites: The leader keeps their hands free

read.plain:
High-performance CPR is the recognition that resuscitation is a team performance, and that teams perform better when everybody knows their job before they walk in.

The pit-crew idea is exactly what it sounds like. In motorsport, nobody discusses who is changing which wheel when the car arrives. Everyone has a position, they move to it, and the work happens in parallel. Resuscitation done well looks the same: compressor, ventilator, defibrillator operator, airway, and a leader, each going to their place without a conversation.

The measurement that matters is compression fraction — what proportion of the whole resuscitation had compressions actually happening. Every pause reduces it, and blood pressure generated by compressions falls away within seconds of stopping and takes several compressions to build back up. That is why pauses are so expensive and why shaving seconds off changeovers is worth rehearsing.

Changeovers get planned. The next compressor is already kneeling in position, hands hovering, and the swap happens on a count during the rhythm check rather than as a negotiation.

And the leader keeps their hands off the patient. Somebody has to be watching the whole thing — the clock, the quality, the plan, the family — and that person cannot also be counting compressions.
read.standard: High-performance cardiopulmonary resuscitation conceptualises resuscitation as a coordinated team performance with pre-assigned roles, eliminating on-scene role negotiation. Roles typically comprise compressor, ventilator, defibrillator operator, airway manager and team leader. The principal quality metric is chest compression fraction, the proportion of resuscitation time during which compressions are delivered; coronary perfusion pressure generated by compressions decays within seconds of cessation and requires multiple compressions to re-establish, rendering interruptions disproportionately costly. Compressor changeover is planned and rehearsed, with the incoming provider positioned in advance and transition executed during rhythm analysis. The team leader maintains a hands-off role to preserve global situational awareness, including timing, quality monitoring, treatment planning and family communication.

eli_new.analogy: A pit crew does not decide who is changing the tyre when the car pulls in.
eli_new.body: The difference between adequate and excellent resuscitation is almost entirely made of seconds that nobody thought were important — a slow changeover, a pause that ran long, a defibrillator that was not ready. Those seconds add up to the compression fraction, and compression fraction tracks survival.

story.title: Everybody knew where to stand
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — arrest, second floor flat, three crews responding.
story.body:
Nine people ended up in a small bedroom and it should have been chaos.

It was not, because the service had drilled positions. Compressor at the chest, next compressor kneeling behind ready, airway at the head, defib operator at the left, officer standing back with a clipboard and no hands on anybody.

The post-call download showed compressions running for over ninety percent of the time they were there. Nobody had to be told anything twice.
