concepts.title: Mechanical CPR devices
key_points: Devices that deliver chest compressions automatically at a set rate and depth
Their advantage is consistency: they do not tire and their quality does not decay
Particularly useful during transport, on stairs, and in prolonged resuscitation
Applying one must not create a long pause in compressions
They are an awareness-level topic for EMTs and their use is governed by local protocol and training
They do not replace the team: everything else in the resuscitation continues around them
misconceptions: Stopping compressions for a long period while positioning a device
Assuming a device removes the need for the rest of the resuscitation
Using a device without service-specific training
exam_favorites: That application must not cause a long pause

read.plain:
Mechanical CPR devices do the compressions for you, at a rate and depth that does not change no matter how long the resuscitation runs.

That consistency is the whole argument for them. A human compressor is at their best for about two minutes and then declines, whatever they believe about themselves. A machine is identical at minute forty to how it was at minute one.

They are most valuable where human compressions are worst: moving a patient down a staircase, in the back of a moving ambulance, and in very long resuscitations. Compressions on the move are nearly always poor, and a device removes that problem.

The risk is in the application. Getting one positioned takes time, and if that time is a pause in compressions you may have given away more than the device gains back. It goes on during a planned pause, quickly, with the team ready.

For an EMT this is an awareness topic. Whether you use one, and how, is set by your service's protocol and training, and a device you have not been trained on is not a device you should be fitting to a patient in arrest.

And it does not replace anybody. Ventilation, defibrillation, the leader, the family — all of that continues exactly as before, with a machine doing one part of it.
read.standard: Mechanical chest compression devices deliver automated compressions at predetermined rate and depth. Their principal advantage is consistency, as device performance does not degrade over time whereas human compression quality declines measurably within approximately two minutes. They are of particular value where manual compression quality is inherently compromised: during extrication, stair descent, transport in a moving vehicle and prolonged resuscitation. Application must be accomplished without prolonged interruption of compressions, as pauses incurred during device positioning may offset the benefit conferred. Device use at EMT level is determined by service protocol and specific training. Mechanical compression substitutes only for manual compression; ventilation, defibrillation, team leadership and family communication continue unchanged.

eli_new.analogy: A person is excellent for two minutes. A machine is identical at minute forty.
eli_new.body: The temptation with any new equipment is to treat getting it on as the goal. The goal is still compressions with minimal interruption; the device is only worth it if fitting it costs less than it gives back.

story.title: On the stairs
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — arrest, fourth floor, no lift.
story.body:
Four flights of narrow stairs with a patient in arrest is where manual compressions go to die. You cannot compress properly on a stretcher going down a turn.

The device went on during a planned pause at the rhythm check — about eleven seconds, and the team had rehearsed it.

All the way down those stairs the compressions were exactly as deep and exactly as fast as they had been in the flat.

concepts.title: Return of spontaneous circulation and post-arrest care
key_points: ROSC means the heart has resumed producing a pulse
Signs include a palpable pulse, a rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide, movement, and sometimes breathing
The patient is still critically unwell; ROSC is the beginning of the next problem, not the end of the call
Reassess airway, breathing and circulation immediately and support whatever is failing
Avoid hyperventilation: it raises pressure in the chest and reduces blood return to a heart that has just restarted
Re-arrest is common in the first minutes, so keep the defibrillator attached and the team in place
Handle gently, keep monitoring, and transport to somewhere that can provide post-arrest care
misconceptions: Treating ROSC as the end of the resuscitation
Hyperventilating a patient after ROSC
Removing the defibrillator pads once a pulse returns

read.plain:
Return of spontaneous circulation is the moment the heart starts producing a pulse again, and it is not the end of anything. It is the start of a different and equally dangerous phase.

You will notice it several ways. A pulse you can feel. A sudden sustained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide, which often comes first. Movement, purposeful or otherwise. Sometimes the patient starts breathing.

The immediate job is to go straight back to the beginning. Airway — is it open, will it stay open, do they need an adjunct. Breathing — are they breathing at all, and adequately, and do you need to ventilate. Circulation — what is the pulse doing, what is the blood pressure, what does the skin look like.

There is one specific trap. The urge after ROSC is to ventilate enthusiastically, because it feels like helping. Do not. Every positive-pressure breath raises the pressure inside the chest and works against blood returning to a heart that has just started again and is extremely fragile. Hyperventilation after ROSC actively harms, and it is a common error made by people who are relieved.

Re-arrest in the first minutes is common. Leave the pads on. Keep the team where they are. Do not start packing up.

And handle them gently. Get them to somewhere that can deliver post-arrest care, which is where a large part of the eventual outcome is actually determined.
read.standard: Return of spontaneous circulation denotes restoration of a perfusing cardiac rhythm and is identified by return of a palpable pulse, an abrupt sustained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide which frequently precedes palpable pulse return, spontaneous movement and sometimes spontaneous respiration. ROSC represents transition to the post-arrest phase rather than resolution, and immediate reassessment of airway, breathing and circulation with support of failing parameters is required. Hyperventilation must be avoided, as elevated intrathoracic pressure impedes venous return to a recently reperfused and haemodynamically fragile myocardium. Re-arrest occurs commonly within the initial post-ROSC period; defibrillation pads remain attached and the resuscitation team remains assembled. Gentle handling, continuous monitoring and transport to a facility capable of delivering post-arrest care are indicated, as post-arrest management substantially determines eventual neurological outcome.

eli_new.analogy: Getting a pulse back is halftime, not the final whistle.
eli_new.body: The emotional shape of the call changes completely at ROSC — relief floods in, people start talking, and the discipline drops. That is exactly the moment the patient is most likely to arrest again.

You recognise it by a palpable pulse, a sudden sustained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide which often comes first, movement, and sometimes spontaneous breathing. Go straight back to airway, breathing and circulation and support whatever is failing. The mistake people make is hyperventilating out of relief: every positive-pressure breath raises the pressure in the chest and works against blood returning to a heart that has only just restarted and is very fragile. Re-arrest in the first minutes is common, so leave the pads on, keep the team in place, handle the patient gently and transport somewhere that can give post-arrest care.

story.title: Halftime
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — arrest, ROSC achieved on scene.

The moment the pulse came back the room got loud. Somebody laughed. Two people started coiling cables.

The officer said, nobody moves, pads stay on, and asked for a blood pressure.

He re-arrested in the ambulance ninety seconds later, and the pads were still on him, and that is the only reason the second shock happened when it did.

concepts.title: When resuscitation is not started or is stopped
key_points: A valid do-not-resuscitate order or equivalent advance directive is a legal instruction and is followed
Obvious signs of irreversible death mean resuscitation is not started — decapitation, decomposition, rigor mortis, dependent lividity, injuries incompatible with life
If a document is not immediately available or its validity is unclear, begin resuscitation while it is sorted out
Starting is reversible; not starting is not
Stopping a resuscitation once begun is generally a physician or protocol decision, not an individual one
Family distress does not change the clinical decision, but how you talk to the family changes everything about how it lands
misconceptions: Withholding resuscitation because a relative says the patient would not want it, with no documentation
Delaying compressions while searching the house for paperwork
Deciding alone to stop a resuscitation you have begun
exam_favorites: That stopping is a protocol decision

read.plain:
There are two situations in which resuscitation is not attempted, and both need to be clear in your head before you are standing in somebody's bedroom at four in the morning.

The first is a valid do-not-resuscitate order or equivalent advance directive. This is a legal instruction from the patient about their own care, and it is followed. Requirements for validity vary by jurisdiction, so know what a valid one looks like where you work.

The second is obvious, irreversible death. The classic signs are decapitation, decomposition, rigor mortis, dependent lividity, and injuries plainly incompatible with life. These are situations where resuscitation is not a close call.

Outside those two, start. And this is the rule worth carrying: if the paperwork is not in front of you, or you cannot tell whether it is valid, or a family member is telling you something but there is nothing to show you, begin resuscitation. Starting a resuscitation that later turns out to have been unwanted is a recoverable situation. Not starting one that should have happened is not.

Do not search the house for a document while a patient is in arrest. Somebody else looks; you compress.

Stopping something you have started is a different decision, and it is generally made by a physician or under a specific protocol, not by one person at the scene.

And separately from all of the above: the family is watching. The clinical decision is not changed by their distress, but how you explain what is happening, and whether you use the person's name, will be remembered for a very long time.
read.standard: Resuscitation is withheld in two circumstances. The first is the presence of a valid do-not-resuscitate order or equivalent advance directive, which constitutes a legal instruction regarding the patient's care; validity criteria are jurisdiction-specific. The second is the presence of signs of irreversible death, conventionally decapitation, decomposition, rigor mortis, dependent lividity and injuries incompatible with life. In all other circumstances resuscitation is initiated. Where documentation is unavailable, incomplete or of uncertain validity, resuscitation is commenced while the position is clarified, on the principle that initiation is reversible whereas omission is not. Searching for documentation must not delay compressions. Termination of resuscitation once commenced is generally a physician decision or governed by specific protocol rather than individual judgement. Family distress does not alter the clinical decision, though communication substantially affects the family's experience of the event.

eli_new.analogy: Starting can be undone. Not starting cannot.
eli_new.body: The pressure in the room at this moment is enormous, and it comes from people who love the patient and are certain about what they would have wanted. Certainty is not documentation. If you are in doubt, your hands go on the chest and somebody else finds the paperwork.

teach.prompt: Explain when you would not start a resuscitation and what you do when the situation is unclear.

must_hit.point: A valid DNR or advance directive is followed
Obvious signs of irreversible death
If unclear or undocumented, start
Starting is reversible; not starting is not
Stopping is a physician or protocol decision

teach.model_answer: You withhold resuscitation in two situations: a valid do-not-resuscitate order or equivalent advance directive, which is a legal instruction and is followed; and obvious irreversible death — decapitation, decomposition, rigor mortis, dependent lividity, injuries plainly incompatible with life. Outside those, you start. If the paperwork is not in front of you, or you cannot judge whether it is valid, or a relative is telling you something without documentation, begin resuscitation while it gets sorted out, because starting is reversible and not starting is not. Do not search the house while someone is in arrest — somebody else looks, you compress. And stopping a resuscitation you have begun is generally a physician or protocol decision rather than yours alone.

story.title: Somebody else looks
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — cardiac arrest, care home, staff performing CPR.
story.body:
A staff member met you at the door saying there was a DNR, definitely, it was in the file, she just could not find which file.

Your partner started compressions. The officer asked her to go and find it and to bring it to him, and she did, and it took about four minutes.

It was valid, and the resuscitation stopped. Had it not been valid, those four minutes would have been the only reason the patient had a chance.

concepts.title: Special resuscitation situations
key_points: Drowning: hypoxia is the cause, so ventilation matters more and rescue breaths come early
Hypothermia: the heart is irritable, so handle gently, check a pulse for longer, and do not assume death until the patient is warm
Pregnancy: manually displace the uterus to the patient's left to take pressure off the major vein returning blood to the heart
Trauma: arrest from major blood loss needs the bleeding controlled and rapid transport; compressions alone move an empty circulation
Electrocution: make the scene safe first, and remember the rescuer is at risk
Overdose: naloxone may reverse an opioid cause but does not replace compressions in arrest
The core of resuscitation does not change; these situations add something, they do not replace it
misconceptions: Delaying compressions to look for the special-case modification
Declaring death in a hypothermic patient before rewarming
Approaching an electrocution scene before the source is isolated
exam_favorites: Not dead until warm and dead

read.plain:
The basics of resuscitation do not change in these situations. Each simply adds something.

Drowning is a hypoxic arrest. The problem started with no oxygen, not with a rhythm, so ventilation carries more weight and rescue breaths come early rather than being an afterthought.

Hypothermia changes two things. A very cold heart is electrically irritable, so handle the patient gently. And a very cold patient may have a pulse so slow and faint that you cannot find it in the usual ten seconds — take longer. There is a saying worth remembering: not dead until warm and dead. Profound hypothermia has produced survivors from situations that looked hopeless, so resuscitation continues and the decision is made later, in hospital.

In late pregnancy the uterus presses on the large vein returning blood to the heart when the patient is on her back, and that pressure alone can prevent effective resuscitation. Somebody manually displaces the uterus to the patient's left. That single action can change whether compressions work at all.

Trauma arrest from blood loss is a different problem: compressions circulate a container that is empty. Controlling catastrophic bleeding and getting to surgery matter more than anything else you can do.

Electrocution begins with the scene, not the patient. If the source is not isolated, the person who goes to help becomes the next patient.

And in overdose, naloxone may address an opioid cause, but a patient in arrest still needs compressions. The antidote is not a substitute for resuscitation.
read.standard: Resuscitation fundamentals remain unchanged in special circumstances, which impose additional considerations. Drowning produces hypoxic arrest, increasing the relative importance of ventilation and indicating early rescue breathing. Hypothermia renders the myocardium electrically irritable, requiring gentle handling, and profound bradycardia with reduced pulse volume necessitates prolonged pulse assessment; resuscitation is continued pending rewarming, as neurologically intact survival has been reported following prolonged hypothermic arrest. In advanced pregnancy, aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus in the supine position impairs venous return, and manual left uterine displacement is performed. Traumatic arrest secondary to exsanguination requires hemorrhage control and expedited transport, as compressions circulate an inadequately filled vascular system. Electrical injury requires isolation of the source prior to patient contact. In opioid toxicity, naloxone may address the underlying cause but does not substitute for chest compressions in established arrest.

eli_new.analogy: Each of these adds one thing to the standard resuscitation. None of them replaces it.
eli_new.body: The risk with special situations is that people go looking for the special part and forget the ordinary part. The compressions still have to be fast, deep and uninterrupted; the modification sits on top of that, not instead of it.

teach.prompt: Describe what changes in resuscitation for drowning, hypothermia and late pregnancy.

must_hit.point: Drowning is hypoxic, so ventilation matters more
Hypothermia: gentle handling, longer pulse check, not dead until warm
Pregnancy: displace the uterus to the left
The fundamentals do not change

teach.model_answer: The basics never change; each of these adds something. Drowning is a hypoxic arrest — the problem began with no oxygen rather than a rhythm — so ventilation carries more weight and rescue breaths come early. In hypothermia the heart is electrically irritable so you handle the patient gently, and the pulse may be so slow and faint that you need longer than the usual ten seconds to find it; resuscitation continues, because someone is not dead until they are warm and dead. In late pregnancy the uterus compresses the large vein returning blood to the heart when she is supine, so somebody manually displaces it to her left, and that alone can decide whether compressions work. Trauma arrest from bleeding needs the bleeding controlled, and electrocution needs the source isolated before anybody approaches.

story.title: Not dead until warm
story.dispatch: Rescue 6 — male pulled from a reservoir, prolonged immersion, water temperature near freezing.
story.body:
He had been in the water a long time and he looked, to everyone standing there, unequivocally dead.

The officer said the sentence out loud so that nobody on that bank had to decide for themselves: not dead until warm and dead.

They resuscitated him the whole way in and handed him over still cold. What happened after that was somebody else's decision to make, with a temperature probe and a warming circuit, and not one made on a riverbank.
